title: Hypergradient spectra and hidden preference transfer
subtitle: BiMuon · Factorization scaling · Regularization and subliminal learning · Lazy Training
intro: Three close readings connect matrix hypergradients, scaling with problem difficulty, and how regularization changes behavioral transfer. Briefs cover author updates and inference budgets; the classic uses an explicit scale to distinguish feature learning from linearized dynamics.

articles.paper: BiMuon: A Geometry-Aware Stochastic Bilevel Optimization Approach
articles.authors: Zhen Qin · Zhiyao Zhang · Yingbin Liang · Jia Liu
articles.title: Polar updates of hypergradients
articles.evidence: Read §3–7, Theorem 1 and the finite-NS condition

blocks.text: Implicit differentiation inserts inverse lower-level curvature into the upper-level gradient. BiMuon orthogonalizes momentum of a matrix hypergradient upstairs while tracking the lower-level solution with stochastic gradients. Derivatives below are matrix operators evaluated at the lower-level solution. [1]

blocks.label: Implicit hypergradient; μ-strong convexity downstairs ensures invertibility
Algorithm schematic; Ĥ is a stochastic Neumann hypergradient estimate
Theorem 1: exact polar on the left, finite NS on the right; R is uniform over the first T iterates

blocks.title: Evidence boundary
blocks.text: Requires sample-level lower strong convexity, Lipschitz/smoothness assumptions, fresh independent unbiased derivatives and specified stepsizes. Finite NS additionally requires a uniform operator error εq<1 throughout the run; a conventional fixed five steps does not automatically ensure it. ε⁻⁴ counts outer iterations, not end-to-end speedup. [1]

articles.paper: Semiprime Factorization with Discrete Diffusion and Beam Search: Scaling Laws
articles.authors: Brendan O’Donoghue · Nenad Tomašev · Volodymyr Mnih · Timothy Nguyen · Dalin Guo · Arun Nair · Kenneth Yang · Alexandre Fréchette · Jasper Xian · Jean Tarbouriech · Pavel Tyletski · Ingrid von Glehn · Johannes Bausch · Demis Hassabis · Raia Hadsell
articles.title: Power-law loss does not remove exponential problem-size scaling
articles.evidence: Read §3–5, Tables 1–2 and relevant appendix setup

blocks.text: Given a semiprime n, discrete diffusion predicts two factors of at most k bits. Repeated remasking on one trajectory and beam search are distinct decoding protocols. Scaling is studied separately in data, model size, denoising steps and k. [2]

blocks.label: Empirical fits: s counts training steps; the last relation approximates a fixed low-loss trend, not a complexity lower bound

blocks.text: For k=15–18, another factor bit needs roughly twice as many training steps. More inference compute helps models already achieving nonzero success, but did not produce exact factors with standalone k=34 decoding. [2]

rows: 109k training steps; up to 16,384 denoising steps; 1,024 tests

blocks.title: Evidence boundary
blocks.text: The 68-bit record is one success combining a diffusion candidate with classical lattice postprocessing, not high solve rates or superiority over classical factoring. Small-k data repeat examples and prime factors; held-out pairs do not imply generalization to unseen primes. [2]

blocks.text: A teacher receives a preference prompt but outputs only number sequences. The student never sees that prompt and only runs SFT; transfer is measured outside the training domain. Lower LoRA rank, parameter penalties and more unique data can each strengthen transfer. [3]

blocks.text: Learning rates are tuned by rank. The table measures direct preference answers, not training accuracy or general safety. Trend strength differs across targets and transfer protocols. Preference complexity determining optimal regularization remains an author hypothesis. [3]

classic.title: How a large scale freezes features
classic.paper: On Lazy Training in Differentiable Programming
classic.authors: Lénaïc Chizat · Edouard Oyallon · Francis Bach
classic.evidence: Read §1–3 and Theorems 2.2–2.4; squared-loss dynamics are an equivalent derivation

recognition.label: NeurIPS 2019 · foundational work on feature learning and kernel limits

classic.question: When comparing Muon with Adam, if parameter displacements are similar but Jacobian-kernel drift differs, which quantity better distinguishes actual feature learning?

blocks.text: NTK (2018) connects wide networks to kernels. This paper shows that width is not the only route to lazy training: explicit output scaling can make a model behave like its initial tangent space. Let h map parameters to a Hilbert prediction space, with locally Lipschitz Dh and Lipschitz gradient of risk R. [13,14]

blocks.label: α⁻² preserves an appropriate dynamical timescale; nonlinear and tangent models share initialization

blocks.tex: \dot w=-\alpha^{-1}Dh(w)^*\nabla R(\alpha h(w)),\quad u=\alpha h(w),\quad \dot u=-K(w)\nabla R(u),\quad K(w)=Dh(w)Dh(w)^*
blocks.label: Chain rule: the Jacobian kernel preconditions prediction-space gradient flow
Equivalent solution for the tangent model: exponential decay in positive-eigenvalue directions; nullspace residual remains
Theorem 2.2: h(w₀)=0, fixed finite T, α→∞; constants can depend on T

blocks.text: Proof route: control parameter displacement, bound kernel drift through local Lipschitzness of Dh, then compare the flows with Grönwall. Strongly convex risk and a surjective initial Jacobian enable a separate all-time result; it does not follow directly from fixed-T bounds. CNN experiments show degraded performance in the lazy regime, not a theorem that every feature-learning model is better. [13]
